1:
Four of them make the same use of Peter being called to account. Barnes says this shows conclusively that the early Christians did not regard him as having any supremacy over the church, since had they held the authority claimed for him they would have submitted at once. Clarke is blunter: the primitive church at Jerusalem, which alone deserves the name, had no conception of his being prince of the apostles, and would not have called his conduct reprehensible had they thought him infallible head of the church. Robertson ends his note by remarking that Peter is plainly not regarded as any kind of pope or overlord, and Henry observes that they were so far from looking on him as infallible that they contended with him, while Peter never insists on being chief of the apostles, being far from the thought of the supremacy his pretended successors claim. Calvin takes a different line, noting that obstinacy for the most part accompanies error, and that these men do not merely hold back but contend with Peter over an action deserving great praise; they had heard that the Gentiles received the word of God, and what should hinder them from embracing men coupled to them by the same Spirit of faith?

Who exactly the objectors were is examined by two. Calvin argues the phrase cannot mean simply the Jews, since at that time none were in Christ's flock at Jerusalem but the circumcised, so there would be nobody to distinguish them from; he adds that it is unlikely the apostles and the moderate among the faithful attempted this combat, since had they been offended they might have conferred with Peter privately, and concludes these were men who made so much of circumcision that they allowed no place in the kingdom to any who had not professed the law. Robertson reports one scholar who confines the phrase to the six brethren who went with Peter, but thinks that unlikely, since all the disciples at Jerusalem were Jews and the whole body cannot be meant either; he takes it as Luke describing by anticipation the beginning of the great controversy, and notes that the apostles are named in the first verse but not the second. Ellicott makes the point historically, that from this time forth those of the circumcision are a distinct section and often a distinct party in the church, and here is the first symptom of the line they were about to take.

On the charge itself Robertson observes that they objected not to Peter's preaching to the Gentiles but to his entering the house and eating there, which is in principle the complaint the Pharisees made against Jesus for eating with publicans and sinners; he adds that the Jews had not only their rules about clean and unclean food but the likelihood that meat at a Gentile table had been offered to an idol. Ellicott notes that the Greek for uncircumcised is more expressive of scorn than the negative English allows, and Robertson calls it contemptuous. Calvin points out that the thing complained of was not forbidden by the law of God but was a tradition from the fathers, and admires that Peter does not say so: he might justly have despised unskilful men who troubled him unjustly, yet he answers mildly as becomes brethren, remembering that he is one of the flock and that every man must be ready to give an account of his doctrine and life as often as the matter requires. Gill adds only that there were by then more churches in Judea than the one at Jerusalem, and that the ascent from Caesarea was some seventy-five miles. Clarke reports a long addition in one manuscript, which has Peter travelling towards Jerusalem for some time, confirming the brethren and speaking of the grace of God as he met them, before the dispute begins.
4:
Why the whole story is told over again is the first question. Ellicott admits that the almost verbal repetition of the narrative of the preceding chapter seems at first sight inconsistent with our common standard of skill in composition, and offers an explanation: Luke probably got the first account from the disciples he met at Caesarea and the second from those at Jerusalem, and the close agreement of the two seemed to him, as indeed it was, a confirmation of the truth of each. Robertson takes the same view from the other side, that Luke evidently considered this defence important and preserves the marks of authenticity, the story coming originally from Peter himself, and he calls the case of Cornelius a test case of primary importance and the first great difficulty of the early church. Barnes draws a lesson from the method rather than the matter: a simple and unvarnished statement of facts is usually the best way of disarming prejudice and silencing opposition, which commonly arises from exaggerated report and dies away not under angry contention but under a plain relation of what happened. Wesley makes the same point of Peter, that he did not take it ill to be questioned nor desire to be treated as infallible, and answered the more mildly because the matter was one he had not readily believed himself.

The small differences from the first telling are what the commentators collect. Ellicott finds a touch of the vividness of personal recollection in the sheet coming even to me, where the earlier account had it let down to the earth, and again in the intense eager gaze recalled in the next verse; Robertson agrees on both, calling them vivid details added by Peter, and notes that the participle now agrees with the sheet rather than with the vessel. Clarke observes that the phrase for setting the matter forth in order is the very style of Luke, and Robertson traces the same word through the other places where it occurs. Robertson also notes that Peter avoids mentioning Cornelius by name or office, and that in telling how the angel bade him be fetched, mentioned now for the third time, he seems anxious to make plain that he did not go of his own initiative but under God's direct orders. Clarke thinks the six brethren were probably present and pointed to as proper persons to confirm what he was saying.

Two of the differences carry weight. On the words rendered nothing doubting, Robertson reports the reading adopted by the critical editors, making no distinction, and observes that the change of voice carries a change of meaning. Ellicott has the better observation: the Greek verb here is the same as the one rendered contended in the second verse, so that Peter, guided by the Spirit, raised no debate of the kind they were raising against him. The other addition is the promise that the household should be saved. Ellicott notes the words are not in the report of the angel's speech in the earlier chapter but may legitimately be thought implied in it, since the prayer of Cornelius had been for salvation and he was told to send for one who should speak to him. Clarke sets the three forms of the message side by side to show how much more explicit this one is, and Robertson infers that Cornelius was unsaved for all his interest in Jewish worship, and that here is household conversion before household baptism. Gill notes that the clause about the angel being seen in his house is well placed, since an angel having entered it, Peter could not be criminal for following, and adds that the word begin is used by Luke to denote the thing rather than the moment, since what followed happened towards the close of the discourse and not at its opening.
16:
The remembered word about the two baptisms is taken two ways. Robertson says Peter now understands the saying as he had not before, a common experience as new experiences of grace open richer veins in God's truth, and concludes that Peter sees water baptism to be merely the symbol of the spiritual baptism in the heart. Calvin will not have it put so bluntly. He grants that the comparison is not between two baptisms but between the minister and the author, man having the sign in his hand while Christ alone waters and regenerates; but he warns that whoever, trusting to this testimony, makes baptism a cold spectacle void of all grace of the Spirit is greatly deceived, since where Christ is joined with the minister and the Spirit with the sign, as much is attributed to the sacraments as is needful. The conjunction, he adds, must not be so confused that men look to the sign rather than the Spirit. Clarke draws another consequence, that the promise had seemed to belong to the apostles alone but Peter took it as made to all believers, so that the promise of the Spirit is given to the whole body of Christians. Ellicott reasons from the greater to the less: if the baptism of the Spirit had been given them, they were admissible to that of water.

On the question that follows two of them pull in opposite directions, and both make it a weapon. Wesley turns it against exclusive rules of communion, breaking out that church governors should consider how bold an usurpation it is on the authority of the supreme Lord of the Church to lay down rules shutting out from worship any whom he has admitted, and wishing the sin may not be laid to those who, with good intention but in over fondness for their own forms, do it continually. Calvin turns the same words the other way, observing that we resist God not only by striving against him but by lingering, and that he who shuts the gate God opens hinders his work as far as in him lies; on which ground he says those who oppose the baptizing of infants make war against God, and magistrates who should assist the martyrs and instead stop their mouths resist likewise. Barnes puts it as experience rather than argument: the best means of destroying prejudice is a powerful revival of religion, in which more erroneous doctrine is overcome than in all the fierce contentions that ever took place. Ellicott and Robertson both note that the Greek makes two questions of it, who was I, and was I able to hinder God; Robertson adds drily that Peter will later play the coward at Antioch on this very point of eating with Gentile Christians.

The silence at the end is read closely. Ellicott notes that the tenses differ, so they first held their peace and then began a continuous utterance of praise, and adds that the approval given at Jerusalem left the Judaisers who afterwards opposed Paul acting against the church from which they pretended to derive their authority. Calvin takes the ceasing as an evident sign of godliness, since men thoroughly instructed touching the will of God cease at once to contend, and distinguishes it from the shame that keeps in the mind what it dares not utter, a dissemblance of modesty rather than docility. Robertson is less sanguine, judging the acquiescence reluctant and the circumcision party likely to have taken it for an exceptional case; he reports a suggestion that the affair decreased Peter's influence at Jerusalem and helped open the way for the leadership of James. Clarke says plainly that not all were ultimately satisfied, pointing to the later disputes. Barnes takes the moment at its largest, that the doors of the church were opened to the entire Gentile world; Gill lists what they had heard.
19:
The persecution is read as the instrument of the mission. Chrysostom puts it sharply: had they made it their express study how best to establish the church they would have done no other thing than this, they dispersed the teachers; and he observes that when Stephen was slain and the apostles scourged, then the Gentiles received the word. Henry says the same of the persecutors, who hoped to prevent the gospel being carried to the Gentile world and only hastened it; those who fled carried their religion with them, declining suffering for a time but not declining service, reserving themselves for further work. Wesley notes that Luke resumes the thread of his narrative in the very words with which he broke it off. Barnes fills in the city, honoured as a Roman colony, a metropolis and an asylum, and follows its history through earthquake, Saracen conquest and crusade to the town of ten thousand it had become in his own day; Ellicott adds that it was destined to supplant Jerusalem as the centre of Christian activity.

Whom the men of Cyprus and Cyrene spoke to is the crux of the chapter, and they divide on both reading and sense. Clarke reports that the reading Greeks rests on a long list of versions and fathers, that a modern editor has admitted it into the text, and that few critics doubt it; otherwise the verse would be doing again what was done already, since the Hellenist Jews had received the gospel long before. Robertson calls Greeks undoubtedly correct and rests on the little word also, which makes no sense on the other reading. Ellicott finds the manuscripts nearly balanced, notes that one great codex has the incomprehensible reading Evangelists, which so far as it goes tells for Hellenists, and turns the scale on internal evidence: the Hellenists were Jews and so already included in the previous verse, whereas the contrast of Jews and Greeks is familiar and gives the note of progress otherwise missing. Barnes and Calvin keep the other reading and reach the same sense by another road, Calvin arguing that since the Jews just mentioned were partly of Cyprus, which counted as part of Greece, Luke must be distinguishing a further class, and that this compels him to expound it of the Gentiles. Henry alone holds out for Hellenist Jews, citing a Hebraist for the view that they were so called as Jews of the corporation of the city, Antioch being a Syrogrecian town.

What the hand of the Lord means is disputed too. Chrysostom takes it plainly of miracles, and answers that they were needed that men might believe. Henry prefers the power of divine grace opening the hearts of the hearers, precisely because many saw the miracles who were not converted, and observes that these were not apostles but ordinary ministers who nevertheless did wonders. Clarke reads it as the energy of God accompanying the preachers, and turns it against ministers who dispute the necessity or deny the being of that influence. Robertson traces the phrase to the Old Testament and takes it for proof of God's approval; then he makes a doctrinal point, that the hand of the Lord is Jehovah's while the Lord to whom they turned is Jesus, so the early disciples put Jesus on a par with Jehovah, his deity being no late development read back into the history. Calvin praises the constancy of preachers delivered as it were out of the midst of death and not afraid to do their duty even with danger, and draws the rule for how far Christians may flee persecution, that they may spend what is left of life in spreading the glory of God; for banished and suspected strangers to be so bold, he adds, came not of flesh and blood. Gill notes only that these were not the apostles but other ministers of the word.
22:
Why Barnabas was the man sent is agreed. Barnes and Robertson both point to his being a native of Cyprus, so that he probably had friends among the men who had begun the work, and Robertson adds that he already led at Jerusalem through his generosity and his championship of Saul. Ellicott thinks the choice determined by the known sympathies of the Son of Consolation, who had been with Paul at Jerusalem and must have known his hopes on this matter. Calvin puts the sending in a harder light: the apostles then bore the whole burden of the kingdom and had to set churches in order everywhere, and since Satan, as soon as he sees a gate opened for the gospel, endeavours to corrupt what is sincere, the greater a church's gifts the more careful it must be, nothing being easier than to corrupt corn in the blade. Clarke observes that this church at Jerusalem was the original and mother church of Christianity and not the church of Rome, and that a church collectively had power to commission any of its members whom God had qualified.

What Barnabas found and did is where the sharpest disagreement lies. Robertson quotes a judgment that a smaller man would have raised difficulties as to circumcision or baptism, and notes that grace brings gladness, the noun and the verb sharing a root. Calvin makes the joy itself the proof, since ambition is always envious and many seek praise by reproving others, being more desirous of their own glory than of Christ's. Ellicott observes that the verb for exhorting is the one from which Barnabas took his name, and that the preacher, having seen the grace of God and rejoiced at it, knew as all true teachers know that man's will can frustrate that grace and that its co-operation in firm resolve was needed to carry the work through. Clarke presses further into open controversy: God gave them the grace, but it was their business to use it, and if they did not the gift would be resumed; it is absurd to talk of being children of God and of absolute final perseverance when the soul has lost that union, nor is there a word in the book of God, fairly understood, which says such a man shall unavoidably rise from his fall. Barnes reads the same phrase as a settled plan formed at the outset, without which there can be no evidence of piety, and Robertson notes that the glow of first enthusiasm often passes after a revival and that persistence was needed in such a pagan city.

On the character of Barnabas the commendations are unanimous and are turned into a portrait of the ministry. Barnes observes that it is not said he was a man of distinguished talents or a splendid preacher but simply a pious humble man of God, and that humble piety will often do more in the conversion of souls than the most splendid talents, since there is nothing on this earth so mighty as goodness. Clarke builds a threefold character of a minister from the three words, and Robertson notes that the word for good ranks higher than the word for righteous, and that Barnabas rose above the racial narrowness his prejudices would have dictated. Ellicott remarks that praise of this kind is rare in the history, thinks Luke the more anxious to record it because he had soon to narrate the contention that parted the two friends, and notices that the words are identical with those used earlier of Stephen. Calvin asks why faith should be named apart from the Spirit whose gift it is, and answers that it is the principal token by which it appeared that Barnabas was full of the Spirit. Gill notes that he had sold what land he had and given the money to the apostles for the common use.
25:
Why Barnabas went to fetch Saul is not stated and Barnes guesses at it: there was a great revival, there was need of additional labour, Saul was in the vicinity and eminently fitted for the work, and probably no other such man was to be had. Gill adds that Saul had been sent to Tarsus to escape the rage of the Grecians who sought to slay him. Calvin admires the self-forgetting of Barnabas, who might have borne the chief sway at Antioch and instead went into Cilicia to fetch a man he knew would be preferred before him, being no whit afraid of being debased by his coming so long as Christ were glorified.

Where the name Christian came from is the sharper question. Clarke argues from the verb, which in the New Testament means to appoint or name by divine direction, that the name is from God and was most likely given through Saul and Barnabas, and calls it the highest character any human being can bear on earth. Barnes canvasses the same senses, grants that the divine communication is the most usual, and yet inclines the other way, since had the apostles conferred it the record would probably have said so rather than simply that they were called; he thinks the Gentiles gave it without intending reproach, and observes that it soon became one, though it is the most honourable appellation that can be conferred on a mortal. Robertson agrees that the Gentiles gave it, since the Jews would not use the word Christ of them and called them Galileans or Nazarenes, while the followers of Christ called themselves disciples, believers, brethren, saints and those of the way; he adds that the word is formed like a Latin adjective though it is Greek, on the pattern of the words for the followers of Herod and of Caesar.

Ellicott traces the later fortunes of the name. Tradition ascribes its origin to the first bishop of Antioch; his successor forms from it the word Christianity as opposed to Judaism, expressing the whole system of faith and life; the term Catholic seems also to have originated in the same city; and the heathen often wrote and explained the word as though it came from a word meaning good, a mistake the Christians accepted as an unconscious witness that they were good and worthy in their lives. He notes too that the word is used as a neutral and respectful term by Agrippa, and later, when it had gained wider currency, as the name that brought the danger of persecution. Henry turns the whole into an examination: the proper meaning of the new name is one who from serious thought embraces the religion of Christ and makes it his chief care to shape his life by Christ's precepts and example, and hence multitudes take the name to whom it does not rightly belong; the name without the reality will only add to our guilt, and he prays that Christians may forget other names and distinctions and love one another as the followers of Christ ought. Calvin makes a further distinction, that there were in very deed Christians at Jerusalem and in Samaria before this, since to be a disciple of Christ is to be a Christian, and Jerusalem was the fountain from which Christianity flowed; but when they began plainly to be called what they were, the use of the name served greatly to set forth the glory of Christ, since by it they referred their whole religion to him alone. Cyril, on the same events, calls Barnabas a good man full of the Holy Ghost, sent as far as Antioch to help on the good work, and Wesley keeps to the facts of the mission.
27:
What a prophet was at this date is settled before the prophecy is examined. Barnes says the word properly denotes one who foretells future events but is sometimes used in the New Testament simply of religious teachers, since teaching was part of the office; these men, however, seem to have been endowed in a remarkable manner, and one of them at least had the power of foretelling. Clarke agrees that the term often means no more than a teacher, but holds that it evidently means here men under divine inspiration who foretold events, and thinks that Agabus was in his ordinary character a teacher or preacher. Henry adds two observations about their coming. They came from Jerusalem, probably because they were not now so much regarded there and saw their work in a manner done; a city infamous for killing the prophets and abusing them is now justly deprived of them. And they came to Antioch because they had heard of the flourishing state of that church, so that those who are faithful in their little are entrusted with more, and the best understanding of scripture predictions is got in the way of obedience to scripture instructions. Gill dates the visit within the year Saul and Barnabas were there.

How far the dearth extended is a small crux of its own. Ellicott says the word means literally the inhabited earth and is used in the New Testament for the Roman empire, and Wesley says the same in a sentence, that the word frequently signifies all the Roman empire and is doubtless so to be taken here. Robertson calls it a common hyperbole for the empire and notes that Josephus appears to restrict the famine to Palestine. Ellicott adds that the prophecy was in part an echo of the words of Christ about famines, and that the whole reign of Claudius was memorable for frequent ones.

Which famine was meant is answered at length by two, and they answer alike. Barnes lists four in the reign of Claudius: one at Rome in his first or second year, arising from the difficulty of importing provisions, on which the emperor spent much in improving the port at the mouth of the Tiber; one in Greece in his ninth year, in which half a bushel of wheat sold for six drachms; a third at Rome late in the reign, which one historian says was so severe it was deemed a divine judgment; and a fourth in Judea, described by Josephus, in which many died for want and Queen Helena sent servants to Alexandria for corn and to Cyprus for dried figs. That fourth, he says, is doubtless the one meant. Clarke reaches the same result and dates it more narrowly, reporting an editor's note that this is the famine foretold by Agabus, that it fell in the fourth consulship of Claudius rather than the second as an earlier scholar had said, and that since Josephus places it under two successive procurators it must have continued several years. Ellicott supplies the same relief from the same queen, a proselyte to Judaism, whose people at Jerusalem were reduced to great distress. Calvin turns from the date to the purpose, listing why God foretells his judgments, that a space may be granted for repentance, that the faithful may arm themselves with patience beforehand, that the obstinacy of the wicked may be convicted, and that all may learn that miseries do not come by chance; the profit of this particular prophecy, he says, appears in the text, since the men of Antioch were pricked forward by it to relieve their brethren. He adds from the Roman historians that crusts were thrown at the emperor's head in the market, and that his fear of stoning made him careful ever after to provide victual.
29:
The collection is read as the first of a long series. Ellicott points out that it was made at once, before the famine came, that Saul and Barnabas were probably active in stirring up the Gentiles to it, and that it was the beginning of that collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem which afterwards filled so much of the apostle's labours and which he regarded as a bond of union between the Jewish and Gentile sections of the church; he suggests too that the generous devotion of the converts at Jerusalem in their first love had left them more exposed than most to poverty. Robertson notes that the worst of the famine came some years later, so the warning stirred them to send the collection on ahead, and that Luke's sentence is a little tangled from his rush of ideas. Clarke thinks these were probably Gentile converts, who considered that they had received their spiritual blessings through the Christians in Judea, and adds the dry historical remark that the community of goods had by this time ceased.

Calvin asks why one people should be succoured rather than all, since the misery was general, and gives three answers: Judea was impoverished by great destructions of war, the rage of the enemies there made the case of the brethren the more wretched, and Paul declares elsewhere that Judea had special necessities which others regarded. But the reason he presses is gratitude, that there is nothing more just than that those should reap earthly things who have sown spiritual things; every man is bent enough on providing for himself and might have objected, why shall I not rather provide for myself, but calling to mind how greatly they are indebted to these brethren they lay that anxiety aside. He finds a double end in the alms, the duty of charity toward the needy and a testimony of how great account they made of the gospel, in that they honoured the place it came from. He notes that the giving was voluntary, no man prescribing a law to another, and that the rule is for each to consider how much is granted him, so that a poor man may have a liberal mind and a small gift be counted a fat and gorgeous sacrifice; and from the word for ministration he draws the point that rich men have abundance on condition of being the ministers of the poor. He observes last that the relief went not to the whole nation but to those of the household of faith, with the proviso that love ought to extend to all mankind and that this is a matter of preference and not of exclusion.

Who the elders were is disputed at the close. Barnes says this is the first mention of elders in the Christian church, doubts that the elders of the synagogue can be meant since a charity for Christians would hardly be entrusted to them, and inclines to think the word denotes no office at all but the aged and prudent members to whom the distribution was committed; he notes that Calvin supposes the apostles intended and thinks that not probable. Clarke offers a third account, that they were probably those who first believed, and reports a division of the primitive disciples into three classes, the eye-witnesses, the firstfruits of the preaching, and their successors, inclining himself to the deacons. Barnes and Wesley both draw the practical inference, Barnes that the obligation to relieve the temporal wants of those from whom we have received spiritual mercies is repeatedly enforced in the New Testament, and Wesley that the brethren in Judea received in this a manifest proof of the reality of the Gentiles' conversion. Gill remarks only that they did not merely determine but executed.
